Two letters invert security thinking. **Non-repudiation** is a security *goal* in STRIDE and a privacy *threat* in LINDDUN; LINDDUN's own guidance notes the two need not conflict, because a part of a system that requires non-repudiation for security should not need deniability for the same data. Decide per data flow which one applies: an audit log of administrator actions should be non-repudiable; a whistleblowing channel should not.

**Detecting** needs no content at all. linddun.org lists observing communication flows, application side effects (temporary files) and system responses, such as a service revealing that a record exists. A sign-up form that answers "this email is already registered" on a sensitive service (a clinic, a dating site) tells anyone that a person uses it.

blocks.title: LINDDUN over the running app's data flow diagram

scenes.caption: The diagram you would draw for STRIDE: an external entity, processes, a store and flows. LINDDUN walks the same elements with privacy threat types.
Linking and identifying: traces in the store link all of one runner's activity, and a trace that starts and ends at one house identifies its owner.
Detecting: the public map reveals that someone exercises in an empty area at all. Non-repudiation: a timestamped trace is evidence of where a person was.
Data disclosure: the followers feed posts full maps by default, including the start point at home. Unawareness: runners may not know their routes feed the public map.
Non-compliance: no impact assessment was done for the public map, and deletion does not reach map tiles. Each badge becomes a threat entry with a mitigation.

blocks.md:
**From threats to mitigations.** Each threat gets an entry, like a STRIDE finding, with the privacy patterns from lesson 12 and the techniques of lessons 6 to 11 as fixes:

- Linking and identifying in the store: hide the first and last few hundred metres of each trace by default; separate account identity from traces.
- Detecting via the map: opt-in only; exclude sparse areas; bound contributions per person and add DP noise.
- Data disclosure in the feed: private-by-default activity posts; clear controls.
- Unawareness: a plain explanation at the point of collection, and a switch that actually removes the data from the map.
- Non-compliance: an impact assessment (lesson 16) before launch.

blocks.code:
# One LINDDUN threat entry, kept in the repository next to the design doc
- id: PRIV-007
  element: heatmap builder (process) and public tiles (flow)
  type: Detecting
  threat: >
    Activity in sparsely used areas reveals that a small group regularly
    exercises there (for example at a military site or a shelter).
  likelihood: high      # tiles are public and easy to inspect
  impact: high          # physical safety of a group
  mitigations:
    - heatmap participation is opt-in (default off)
    - cells need >= 100 distinct users over 90 days, and sparse regions are excluded
    - at most one contribution per person per cell per day, plus DP noise
  owner: maps-team
  status: open
blocks.caption: A threat register entry in YAML. The format is illustrative; LINDDUN does not mandate one.

blocks.md: **Lean or thorough.** linddun.org offers several methods: **LINDDUN GO**, a card deck for a lean, workshop-style session in which each card describes a threat to look for, and more systematic flavours that walk every element of the data flow diagram against threat trees. Teams new to privacy threat modelling usually start with GO cards at design review.
Do not treat LINDDUN as a compliance checklist. Its value is the same as STRIDE's: asking each element and flow "how could this hurt the people in the data?" before the design is fixed.

LINDDUN: Linking, Identifying, Non-repudiation, Detecting, Data disclosure, Unawareness and unintervenability, Non-compliance. Apply it to the same data flow diagram as STRIDE; it finds harms that need no attacker and no security failure.

blocks.question: A mental health app's password reset page says 'No account found for this email' for unknown emails. Which LINDDUN threat type does this most directly create?
options: Data disclosure
Non-compliance
Unawareness
Detecting
blocks.explain: The response reveals whether a person has an account at all, which on a mental health service is sensitive. That is detecting through system responses. A uniform response ('If an account exists, we sent an email') removes it.

blocks.question: Why is non-repudiation a threat in LINDDUN when it is a security goal in STRIDE?
options: LINDDUN disagrees with STRIDE about logging
Because for users, undeniable evidence of what they did or said can harm them, for example read receipts or signed records of a vote
Because non-repudiation requires encryption
Because GDPR forbids audit logs
blocks.explain: Evidence that protects a system (an admin audit log) can harm an individual where deniability matters. The designer decides per flow which property applies.

lessons.title: Private set intersection: comparing lists without sharing them

blocks.md:
Many features need the overlap of two sets held by different parties. Which of my contacts use this app? Is my password in a breach corpus? Which of our customers are also on a partner's list? The naive way sends one whole list to the other side. **Private set intersection** (PSI) protocols let two parties learn the common items, and nothing more about each other's sets. PSI is one of the **privacy-enhancing technologies** (PETs): techniques that let data be used for a purpose while revealing less of it. Lesson 15 covers another.

Tiny example: Ana's phone has 300 contacts; the messaging server has millions of registered numbers. Ana should learn which of those 300 are registered; the server should not learn Ana's address book.

**Why hashing is not enough.** Signal's 2017 post on contact discovery describes its older design: the app sent truncated SHA-256 hashes of every phone number in the address book, and the server returned the matches. As lesson 3 showed, phone numbers are a small space, so the server (or anyone who breaks into it) can invert the hashes. Signal's answer at the time was not a PSI protocol but an **enclave**: contact discovery runs inside Intel SGX (Software Guard Extensions), isolated hardware memory, and clients use **remote attestation** to verify that the enclave runs the published code before sending their contacts. The post lists private set intersection among the options that did not work for Signal at its scale. Both approaches move trust off the operator; they differ in what you must trust instead.

**PSI from Diffie-Hellman.** Recall from *Cryptography for engineers* that exponentiation modulo a prime commutes: $(g^a)^b = (g^b)^a$. Replace $g$ with the hash of an item, and each party's secret exponent becomes a **blinding** key:

1. Ana sends $H(x)^a$ for each of Ana's items. The server cannot undo $a$.
2. The server returns each value raised to $b$, giving $H(x)^{ab}$, in the same order, and sends its own items as $H(y)^b$.
3. Ana raises the server's values to $a$, giving $H(y)^{ba}$. Equal items give equal values, so Ana sees which positions match.

blocks.title: Diffie-Hellman PSI between a phone and a server

scenes.caption: Ana blinds each contact with a secret exponent a. To the server these are random-looking numbers.
The server adds its own blinding b and returns the values in the same order. It still learns nothing about which numbers they are.
The server sends its registered users blinded with b. Without b, Ana cannot read the server's list.
Ana raises those to a and compares with the doubly blinded list: matches are the intersection. Each side learns the other's set size, and Ana learns the overlap.

blocks.code:
import hashlib, secrets

P = 2**127 - 1                       # a prime; real systems use elliptic curves

def h(item: str) -> int:             # hash an item to a number mod P
    return int.from_bytes(hashlib.sha256(item.encode()).digest(), "big") % P

ana_contacts = ["+15550001", "+15550002", "+15550003"]
server_users   = ["+15550002", "+15550003", "+15550009", "+15550010"]

a = secrets.randbelow(P - 2) + 1     # Ana's secret exponent
b = secrets.randbelow(P - 2) + 1     # server's secret exponent

# 1. Ana blinds each item: H(x)^a
msg1 = [pow(h(x), a, P) for x in ana_contacts]
# 2. Server raises them to b (same order) and sends its own items blinded: H(y)^b
msg2 = [pow(v, b, P) for v in msg1]
msg3 = {pow(h(y), b, P) for y in server_users}
# 3. Ana raises the server's values to a: (H(y)^b)^a == (H(x)^a)^b when x == y
server_double = {pow(v, a, P) for v in msg3}
found = [x for x, v in zip(ana_contacts, msg2) if v in server_double]
print("in both sets:", found)

# Output:
# in both sets: ['+15550002', '+15550003']
blocks.caption: Simplified: a Mersenne prime group and a plain hash for readability. Real deployments use elliptic curve groups and hash-to-curve functions.

blocks.md:
**What it hides and what it does not.** Each side learns the size of the other's set; Ana learns the intersection. A dishonest client could put a guess ("is my ex registered?") into its set, so deployments cap set sizes and rate-limit queries. And when the server's set is huge, sending all of $H(y)^b$ is impractical, so real systems combine PSI with bucketing.

**Case: Google's Password Checkup.** Kurt Thomas and colleagues at Google and Stanford (the USENIX Security Symposium, 2019) built a breach alerting protocol over more than 4 billion breached usernames and passwords. The client hashes the credential with Argon2 (a deliberately slow password hash), sends a short hash prefix that places it in a large **anonymity set** (a k-anonymity bucket), and the two sides compare blinded values using the commutative property of elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman, a PSI. In their Chrome extension study, from nearly 670,000 users and 21 million logins, 1.5 percent of logins used breached credentials, and 26 percent of warnings led users to change to a new password.
PSI reveals set sizes and the intersection, and it cannot stop a party from choosing what goes into its own set. Cap sizes, rate-limit, and log query volumes per client to detect enumeration.

Diffie-Hellman PSI works because blinded exponentiation commutes: H(x)^(ab) = H(x)^(ba). Each side blinds with a secret it never reveals, so only matching items line up. Hashing alone is not PSI, because hashes of small identifier spaces can be inverted.

blocks.question: In the DH-PSI protocol, why can the server not learn Ana's contacts from H(x)^a?
options: Because H(x)^a is encrypted with TLS
Because the server deletes the values
Because SHA-256 cannot be inverted
Because it can hash any guessed number, but comparing H(guess) with H(x)^a needs Ana's secret a, and finding a from the values it sees is a discrete logarithm problem
blocks.explain: The server could hash every phone number, but it cannot compare those hashes to H(x)^a without knowing a. That is the difference from plain hashing, which a server can test guesses against.

blocks.question: Which of these does a basic PSI protocol still reveal?
options: Nothing at all
The other party's full set
The sizes of the two sets, and the intersection to the receiving party
The other party's secret exponent
blocks.explain: Set sizes are visible from the number of blinded values, and the receiving party learns the common items by design. Padding sets and rate limits reduce what this leaks.

lessons.title: Secure aggregation: a server that learns only the sum

blocks.md:
Some systems need only a total over many users: the sum of model updates in federated learning (training a shared model while data stays on phones), or a count of how many users saw a crash. **Secure aggregation** lets a server compute the sum of users' values without seeing any individual value.

Tiny example: three phones hold 5, 3 and 9. The server should learn 17 and nothing else. If each phone adds a random-looking mask, and the masks are designed to cancel when added up, the server sees three random numbers that sum to 17.

Keith Bonawitz and colleagues at Google described a practical protocol (*Practical Secure Aggregation for Federated Learning on User-Held Data*, 2016, with a full paper in 2017). Its first step, **masking with one-time pads** (from *Cryptography for engineers*: a random pad hides a value perfectly):

- Each pair of users $u < v$ agrees on a random value $s_{u,v}$.
- User $u$ adds $s_{u,v}$ for every partner with a higher id and subtracts it for every partner with a lower id, all modulo $R$.
- Each pair's values appear once with a plus and once with a minus, so in the server's sum they cancel.

blocks.tex: y_u = x_u + \sum_{v > u} s_{u,v} - \sum_{v < u} s_{v,u} \pmod R, \qquad \sum_u y_u = \sum_u x_u \pmod R
blocks.caption: Each pair secret is added by one user and subtracted by the other. In the full protocol pairs derive s from a Diffie-Hellman key agreement and a pseudorandom generator.

blocks.code:
import random

R = 1000                                   # all arithmetic is mod R
x = {1: 5, 2: 3, 3: 9}                     # each phone's private value
random.seed(3)
# each pair (u < v) agrees on a shared random value s[u, v]
# (in the real protocol: from a Diffie-Hellman key agreement and a PRG)
s = {(u, v): random.randrange(R) for u in x for v in x if u < v}
print("pair secrets:", s)

def masked(u):
    y = x[u]
    for (a, b), secret in s.items():
        if u == a: y += secret             # the lower id adds
        if u == b: y -= secret             # the higher id subtracts
    return y % R

y = {u: masked(u) for u in x}
print("server receives:", y)
print("sum of masked values:", sum(y.values()) % R, "true sum:", sum(x.values()))
print("if phone 3 drops out:", (y[1] + y[2]) % R)

# Output:
# pair secrets: {(1, 2): 243, (1, 3): 606, (2, 3): 557}
# server receives: {1: 854, 2: 317, 3: 846}
# sum of masked values: 17 true sum: 17
# if phone 3 drops out: 171
blocks.caption: Three phones, modulus 1000. The server sees 854, 317 and 846, which reveal nothing on their own, and their sum mod 1000 is the true total 17.

blocks.title: Pairwise masks cancelling in the sum (mod 1000)

scenes.caption: Phones 1, 2 and 3 hold 5, 3 and 9. Pairs agreed secrets: s12 = 243, s13 = 606, s23 = 557.
Net masks: phone 1 adds 243 + 606 = 849; phone 2 adds 557 and subtracts 243, so 314; phone 3 subtracts 606 + 557, so -1163.
Each phone sends value plus mask mod 1000: 854, 317, 846. Each looks uniformly random to the server.
The masks sum to 849 + 314 - 1163 = 0, so 854 + 317 + 846 = 2017, which is 17 mod 1000: the true total, and only the total.

blocks.prompt: Phone 3 loses its connection before sending. The server adds the two values it received. What does it get?
blocks.reveal: 854 + 317 = 1171, which is 171 mod 1000: garbage. Phone 1 and 2's masks with phone 3 (606 and 557) no longer cancel. The protocol must survive users dropping out, which is the job of the next step.

blocks.md:
**Dropouts and a dishonest server.** The paper adds two refinements:

- **Secret sharing for dropouts.** Each user splits its mask secrets with **Shamir's secret sharing** (Adi Shamir, 1979: a secret split into n shares so that any t of them rebuild it, but fewer reveal nothing) and gives shares to the others. If a user drops out, the survivors send shares so the server can rebuild that user's pair masks and remove them.
- **Double masking.** That creates a risk: a server could falsely claim an honest user dropped out, collect the shares, and unmask that user's value. So each user also adds a second, self-chosen mask $b_u$, also secret-shared. For each user, an honest participant will release shares of either the pair masks (user dropped) or $b_u$ (user survived), never both.

Pair secrets come from a Diffie-Hellman key agreement, expanded with a pseudorandom generator, so each user only shares one key instead of one secret per partner.

**What secure aggregation does not protect.** The server still learns the sum, and a sum can reveal a person: with two contributors, each can subtract their own value and learn the other's. So production systems set a minimum number of contributors per round, and add differential privacy noise to the sum (lesson 10's secure computation trust model) when the output itself must not reveal any one user.

Related tools: **homomorphic encryption** lets a server compute on ciphertexts without decrypting them, at a higher computational cost; trusted execution environments (Signal's enclave in lesson 14) instead move trust to hardware and its attestation.

Secure aggregation: pairwise masks that cancel in the sum hide each value from the server; secret sharing handles dropouts; double masking stops a server from faking dropouts. The total is still revealed, so require many contributors and add DP noise when the total must not identify anyone.

blocks.question: In the pairwise masking scheme, why does the server learn nothing from a single masked value y_u?
options: Because y_u includes uniformly random pair secrets the server does not know, which act as a one-time pad on x_u
Because y_u is encrypted with TLS
Because the server deletes y_u after summing
Because x_u is always small
blocks.explain: Adding a uniformly random value mod R is a one-time pad: y_u is uniformly distributed whatever x_u is. Only the sum, where the pads cancel, carries information.

blocks.question: A round of secure aggregation has exactly two participants. One of them is curious. What can they learn?
options: The other participant's exact value, by subtracting their own from the published sum
Nothing, secure aggregation hides all inputs
Only the other participant's mask
Only the number of participants
blocks.explain: Secure aggregation hides inputs from the server, not from the meaning of the output. With two inputs, the sum minus your own value is the other's value. Hence minimum cohort sizes and DP noise on the output.

lessons.title: Data protection impact assessments that change the design

blocks.md:
A **DPIA** (data protection impact assessment) is the privacy counterpart of a security design review: a documented assessment, done *before* processing starts, of what could go wrong for the people in the data and what the design does about it. A good DPIA changes the design; a bad one describes a finished system.

Tiny example: before launching the public heatmap, the team writes down what it does, why it is needed, who could be harmed and how, and which mitigations reduce each risk. The lesson 13 threat list feeds straight into it.

blocks.code:
WP248_CRITERIA = [
    "evaluation or scoring", "automated decision with legal or similar effect",
    "systematic monitoring", "sensitive or highly personal data",
    "large scale", "matching or combining datasets",
    "vulnerable data subjects", "innovative technology",
    "prevents exercising a right or using a service",
]

def screen(feature: str, met: set) -> str:
    unknown = met - set(WP248_CRITERIA)
    assert not unknown, unknown
    n = len(met)
    verdict = "DPIA in most cases" if n >= 2 else "judge case by case, record why"
    return f"{feature}: {n} criteria -> {verdict}"

print(screen("global heatmap of all runs",
             {"large scale", "sensitive or highly personal data",
              "matching or combining datasets", "systematic monitoring"}))
print(screen("dark-mode preference sync", set()))

# Output:
# global heatmap of all runs: 4 criteria -> DPIA in most cases
# dark-mode preference sync: 0 criteria -> judge case by case, record why
blocks.caption: A screening helper using the WP248 criteria. Which criteria a feature meets is a judgement; the code only makes the judgement explicit and recorded.

blocks.md: **A practical process.** The UK regulator, the ICO (Information Commissioner's Office), structures its DPIA guidance in seven steps: decide whether a DPIA is needed; describe the processing; consider consultation; assess necessity and proportionality; identify and assess risks; identify measures to mitigate them; conclude and record the outcome. (The ICO notes that this guidance is under review after the UK's Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, which amends UK data protection law.) Risks are usually scored by likelihood and severity of harm *to individuals*, the same grid as a security risk register but with a different victim.

blocks.title: Heatmap DPIA: risk scores before and after measures (illustrative)

scenes.caption: Before measures, scored 1 to 3 for likelihood and severity of harm to people. Revealing a group's location (the Strava case) is likely and severe: 9.
Opt-in by default, excluding sparse regions and bounding contributions with DP noise cut the group-location likelihood to 1: score 3.
Hiding route start and end points by default cuts the home-address risk; separating identity from traces cuts re-identification; a clear notice cuts unawareness.
Residual risks are recorded and signed off. Severity often stays high (location harms are serious); the measures work on likelihood. If any stayed high, Article 36 consultation would apply.

blocks.md: A DPIA written after launch, or one whose risk section lists only security threats to the company, misses the point. It must be done before processing, assess necessity, and score harm to the individuals in the data.

DPIA: required before likely high-risk processing (GDPR Art. 35; WP248: two of nine criteria usually means yes). It must describe the processing, test necessity and proportionality, assess risks to people and record measures; unmitigated high risk goes to the regulator first (Art. 36).

blocks.question: A team launches a feature, then writes a DPIA three months later 'for the file'. What is the main problem?
options: DPIAs must be written by lawyers
DPIAs expire after three months
Only regulators may write DPIAs
Article 35 requires the assessment prior to the processing, so its findings can still change the design
blocks.explain: The duty applies before processing starts, and the point is to change the design while that is cheap. An after-the-fact DPIA can still help, but the launch was out of line with Article 35.

blocks.question: Under Article 35(7), which question belongs in a DPIA but not in a typical security review?
options: Is the data encrypted at rest?
Which CVEs affect the servers?
Is this processing necessary and proportionate to its purpose, or would less data do?
Is multi-factor authentication enabled?
blocks.explain: Necessity and proportionality ask whether the processing should happen at this scale at all. Encryption, patching and MFA are security measures that a DPIA may list, but they do not answer that question.

lessons.title: Rights in code: access and erasure across every copy

blocks.md:
Privacy law gives people rights over their data, and each right is an engineering requirement on every system that holds it. The two that hurt most if the architecture ignores them are access (give me a copy of everything you hold about me) and erasure (delete it).

Tiny example: a user asks to be deleted. Their row disappears from the accounts table. Their runs stay in object storage, their pseudonym in analytics, their email in five support tickets and their data in last night's backup. The request has been answered, and not fulfilled.

**What the GDPR asks.**

- **Article 15, right of access**: confirmation of whether data is processed and a copy, plus the purposes, the categories of data, the recipients, the retention period or the criteria for it, and the existence of the other rights.
- **Article 17, right to erasure** ("right to be forgotten"): erase without undue delay on grounds including that the data is no longer necessary for its purposes or that consent was withdrawn, with exceptions such as legal claims (17(3)(e)), which is why a legal hold pauses erasure.
- [Article 12(3)](https://gdpr-info.eu/art-12-gdpr/), **the clock**: act on a request without undue delay and in any event within **one month** of receipt, extendable by two further months for complex or numerous requests, telling the person within the first month.
- **Article 30**: controllers keep a **record of processing activities** (purposes, categories of data and people, recipients), which is the starting point for knowing where data lives.

**The engineering core is a data map.** Manageability (lesson 1) means you can find all of one person's data. That needs, for every system holding personal data: which key finds a person there (user id, email, pseudonym), how to export from it, and how to erase from it. Without the map, each request becomes a manual search that misses copies.

**Backups.** The [ICO's erasure guidance](https://ico.org.uk/for-organisations/uk-gdpr-guidance-and-resources/individual-rights/individual-rights/right-to-erasure/) says erasure must also reach backups, but accepts that data may remain there until overwritten if it is put **beyond use**: not used for any other purpose and held only until replaced on an established schedule, and the person must be told clearly what happens to it. Restores must then re-apply pending erasures. Another answer is crypto-shredding: encrypt data under per-dataset or per-person keys and destroy the key (the data security course shows it for backups).

blocks.code:
# Data map: every system that holds personal data, and how to erase from it
SYSTEMS = {
    "accounts_db":  {"key": "user_id", "erase": "delete row"},
    "runs_bucket":  {"key": "user_id", "erase": "delete objects"},
    "analytics":    {"key": "pseudonym", "erase": "delete by pseudonym"},
    "support_desk": {"key": "email", "erase": "redact tickets"},
    "backups":      {"key": None, "erase": "expires with backup cycle"},
}

def erasure_plan(user: dict) -> list:
    plan = []
    for name, s in SYSTEMS.items():
        if s["key"] is None:
            plan.append(f"{name}: beyond use: {s['erase']}, re-apply erasures after any restore")
        else:
            plan.append(f"{name}: {s['erase']} where {s['key']} = {user[s['key']]}")
    return plan

for step in erasure_plan({"user_id": 812, "pseudonym": "p_9f3a", "email": "ana@example.org"}):
    print(step)

# Output:
# accounts_db: delete row where user_id = 812
# runs_bucket: delete objects where user_id = 812
# analytics: delete by pseudonym where pseudonym = p_9f3a
# support_desk: redact tickets where email = ana@example.org
# backups: beyond use: expires with backup cycle, re-apply erasures after any restore
blocks.caption: A data map drives the erasure plan. The analytics pseudonym can only be found because the service that holds the pseudonym key can compute it.

blocks.title: One erasure request against the one-month clock

scenes.caption: Day 0: the request arrives through any channel (support email counts). The one-month clock starts on receipt.
If there is doubt about who is asking, the ICO allows asking for proportionate proof of identity; the request need not be fulfilled until it arrives.
The data map fans the request out: accounts, runs, analytics by pseudonym, support tickets, partners the data was shared with.
Backups are put beyond use until they expire; the reply explains this. Done well inside one month, with evidence of each step kept for audit.

blocks.md:
**Defender's view: rights requests are an attack surface.** An access request is a way to obtain someone's full data, so an impostor who can pass as the user gets everything. Verify identity in proportion to what you hold: a request from inside a logged-in session with recent re-authentication is strong; an email from a new address claiming to be the user is weak. Log every request and export, alert on bursts of requests, and send the export only to a verified channel.

**Design payoff.** Everything minimised in lesson 12 is something you never have to find, export or erase. Truly anonymous outputs, such as DP statistics, are not personal data and need no erasure; pseudonymised data does.
Deleting the primary row is not erasure. Without a data map, copies in analytics, tickets, partners and backups survive, and the reply you sent the user is false.

Rights are requirements on every copy: build a data map (system, lookup key, export method, erase method), meet the one-month clock (Art. 12(3)), put backups beyond use, notify recipients, and verify identity in proportion to what you would hand over.

blocks.question: A user's erasure request arrives on 3 March. Absent an extension, by when must the controller act on it under Article 12(3)?
options: Within 72 hours
Within three months
Within one year, at the next retention review
Within one month of receipt, so by early April
blocks.explain: Article 12(3): without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt, extendable by two further months for complex or numerous requests if the person is told within the first month. 72 hours is the breach notification clock.

blocks.question: An attacker emails support from a lookalike address asking for 'all data you hold about me' for a victim's account. What control matters most?
options: Encrypting the export
Verifying the requester's identity in proportion to the data, for example by requiring the request from the authenticated account
Replying within one month
Deleting the data instead
blocks.explain: The risk is disclosure to an impostor. Proportionate identity verification (the ICO allows asking for information needed to confirm identity) and delivery to a verified channel prevent it; encryption does not help if you send it to the attacker.

lessons.title: Putting it together: a privacy review, and where to practise

blocks.md:
This lesson runs the whole course on one feature, the public heatmap, in the order a privacy engineer would.

1. **Map the data actions** (lesson 1): collect GPS traces, store, aggregate, publish tiles. The objectives at risk: predictability (do runners expect this?) and disassociability (can tiles be tied to people or groups?).
2. **Threat-model with LINDDUN** (lesson 13): linking and identifying in the store, detecting through sparse tiles, data disclosure in feeds, unawareness of the map.
3. **Screen and run a DPIA** (lesson 16): large scale, location data, combining datasets; it is needed. Necessity: does the map need every runner, or only those who opt in?

4. **Choose techniques by what must be released** (lessons 2 to 11):
   - Individual records to outsiders? Avoid. Names removed, hashes, pseudonyms and k-anonymity all failed in this course's cases (GIC, AOL, Netflix).
   - Aggregates? Use differential privacy with user-level bounds and a recorded budget; check the trust model and use a vetted library.
   - A comparison between two parties' sets? PSI. A sum across many devices? Secure aggregation, with a minimum cohort and DP on the result.
5. **Minimise by design** (lesson 12): opt-in, coarsen, hide trace endpoints, purpose-bind fields, enforce with grants.
6. **Plan for rights** (lesson 17): the tiles are DP aggregates and need no per-person erasure; the traces do.
7. **Test the release** before and after launch: look at the emptiest places on your own map, as Nathan Ruser did.

blocks.title: Choosing a privacy technique for a data release

nodes.label:
Secure aggregation
+ DP on the sum

scenes.caption: Start from what must leave the system, not from the data you have. Most features need far less than full records.
Records about individuals: removing names, hashing and k-anonymity all failed in this course's cases. Minimise, or share under contract in a controlled environment.
Statistics: differential privacy with a user-level unit, a public budget and a vetted library, as the 2020 Census did.
Comparisons and sums: PSI and secure aggregation keep inputs hidden, but their outputs (overlap, total) still need limits and sometimes DP.

blocks.md: **Where to read next.** CyBOK (the Cyber Security Body of Knowledge, a free reference curriculum) has a Privacy and Online Rights knowledge area. The NIST Privacy Framework is, in NIST's words, a voluntary tool to help organizations identify and manage privacy risk; it sits beside the NIST CSF from *Risk, governance and compliance for engineers*, and version 1.1 is in draft. NIST SP 800-226 is the reference for reviewing differential privacy claims.

**Practise legally, on your own data and tools:**

- Work through the [OpenDP documentation](https://docs.opendp.org/en/stable/) and release DP counts and means from a public dataset; compare errors at several epsilons with this course's 95 percent formula.
- Read the examples in [Google's differential privacy libraries](https://github.com/google/differential-privacy) and find where contributions are bounded.
- Run a LINDDUN session on an app you build, using the [LINDDUN GO cards](https://linddun.org/linddun-go/) and the [threat types](https://linddun.org/threat-types/).
- Map one of your projects to the [NIST Privacy Framework](https://www.nist.gov/privacy-framework) and the [CyBOK knowledge base](https://www.cybok.org/).
- Re-run this course's code (uniqueness, k-anonymity, Laplace noise, PSI, secure aggregation) on synthetic data and change the parameters.

Re-identification research on real people's data needs an ethics review and the data holder's permission; never test linking attacks on data about others you have not been authorised to study.

A privacy review asks, in order: what data actions happen, how they could hurt people (LINDDUN), whether the processing is necessary (DPIA), what must leave the system and the matching technique (DP, PSI, secure aggregation, or not releasing), how the design minimises, and how rights reach every copy.

blocks.question: A partner asks for 'anonymised' per-user listening histories to build a recommender. Which response best follows this course?
options: Hash user IDs and send the histories
Avoid releasing records: offer DP aggregates, or let the partner's code run in a controlled environment on your side
k-anonymise the histories at k = 5 and send them
Remove names and send a 10 percent sample
blocks.explain: Sparse behavioural histories are re-identifiable even without identifiers (Netflix), hashing is reversible on known IDs (lesson 3), k-anonymity fails on high-dimensional data, and sampling did not help Netflix. Releasing no records is the robust option.

blocks.question: Which pair of facts should a reviewer always ask for when a team says a release is differentially private?
options: The encryption algorithm and key size
The number of rows and columns
The epsilon (and delta) and the unit of privacy, plus who sees raw data
The DPIA author's name
blocks.explain: Epsilon and delta give the strength, the unit of privacy says whom it protects (events or people), and the trust model says whether a curator could leak raw data anyway. Without these, 'DP' is a label, not a guarantee.
